reader.notes: ScreenAdvancingCount admits an integer literal not written with '-' and figurative ZERO, refusing every other literal (COBOL2365). Two readings left open, not counted against the rule: the amended 1985 glossary says integer 'must be neither signed nor zero unless explicitly allowed', so a strict reader could refuse +2; and figurative ZERO is admitted as integer-1 although 1985 permits a figurative constant where 'literal' appears in a format. Both are the same code at 2023.

refuter.evidence: r6a.cob (r6a-001): ADVANCING ZEROES LINES, ADVANCING ZEROS, ADVANCING +0 LINES and ADVANCING +3 LINES all compile and run (LC=004); reader's w5b shows -0 refused (COBOL2365). Code: SequentialIoBinder.ScreenAdvancingCount admits any integer literal not starting with '-' and BoundFigurative Kind 'Z', citing §2023 text only, no 1985 arm. The 1985 text: cite.py OK §1985:III.2 "Where the term 'integer' appears in the general formats, integer must be a numeric literal which is an integer, and it must be neither signed nor zero unless explicitly allowed by the rules for that format."; OK §1985:IV.4.2.2.2.3 "A figurative constant may be used whenever 'literal' appears in a format"; OK §1985:VII.4.7.3 SR5 "may be positive or zero, but must not be negative". Readings: (1) ZERO/ZEROS/ZEROES: integer-1 is the format term 'integer', not 'literal', and no 1985 rule licenses a figurative constant where 'integer' appears, so a strict reading refuses it (under-rejects); the other reading treats 'integer' as a numeric literal and applies the figurative rule's exception (1) (only ZERO). (2) Signs: SR5 explicitly allows zero but does not explicitly allow a sign; under the strict reading +3 and +0 must be refused (under-rejects); under the permissive reading (SR5's 'must not be negative' contemplates a sign) the value decides, and -0 (value zero, §1985:IV numeric literal value is the algebraic quantity) is legal and its COBOL2365 refusal rejects legal source. No single reading of the 1985 text makes both '+3 accepted' and '-0 refused' right. The verdict rests on a reading the text does not settle.
